result:
I stopped at the 15-minute search budget with 8 of the 24 scorer calls used. The final answer is in `final.py` and scores **85.0** on the search split, against about 1.0 for the baseline. The same code scored 86.1 on an earlier call, so the scorer varies by about ±1–2 between runs.

| | search score |
|---|---|
| baseline | ~1.0 |
| first champion (c1) | 68.3 |
| **final pick (c17 = final.py)** | **86.1, confirmed at 85.0** |

**Held-out:** the scorer only exposes the search split, so the real held-out score comes later. On my own generator, using seeds I never tuned on, the final code reports exactly the reference's pairs and runs 91× faster. I also tested inputs where most words are shared across records, which is the worst case for this method. It stayed correct and was still 3–11× faster than the reference, well clear of the cut-off at 3× slower. The edge cases (empty input, blank records, repeated words, whitespace variants) all match.

**Why it's faster.** The baseline compares every pair of records. The new version compares only the few pairs that could possibly reach 80 %:
- **Identical records** are grouped first; every pair within a group is reported straight away.
- **Records of 1–3 words** can only match an identical record, so they skip the rest of the work.
- **Each remaining record is indexed by only its few rarest words.** Two records can only be 80 % alike if they share one of these. Records are processed from shortest to longest, and size limits cut the list further, so only about 12k pairs get the exact check.
- **What the time goes on now** is mostly splitting the text and building the word sets. The last gains came from small things: estimating word frequency from every 4th record, and leaving out the `collections` import, which cost about 1 ms of the ~16 ms run.

**Other approaches tried:**
- **Two tiers of words (rare, then common)** instead of a full frequency order: 17× more candidate pairs and slower; dropped.
- **Skipping records with too many unique words:** scored 62.5; few records qualify, so the extra check cost more than it saved.
- **Importing from the private `_collections` module:** the scorer rejects this as not allowed.

**Candidate log** (calls left: 16, minutes left: 0)
```
c1  rare-word index, rank order        harness 78x  score 68.3  kept
c3  shorter index lists for smaller records  82x    —           folded in
c4  Counter + sort on integer ranks    90x          —           kept
c5  C-level grouping, merged loops     91x          score 78.0  kept
c6  two-tier word order                34.6 ms (vs 19)  —       dropped (candidates 11k→189k)
c7  skip records with many unique words  23.8 ms    score 62.5  dropped
c8–c11  private _collections import    ~96x         invalid     dropped (not allowed)
c10 grouping via dict(zip)             no gain      —           dropped
c12 c11 using public Counter           91x          score 77.5  kept
c14 skip records of 1–3 words          96x          score 82.0  champion
c15 drop collections import            ≈c14         —           base for c17
c16 dedupe identical strings first     ≈c15         —           dropped
c17 sampled counting + size tables     20.4 ms      score 86.1 / 85.0  FINAL
c18 C-level candidate gathering        20.9 ms      —           dropped
stride tuning 2/3/4/6/8 → 4 best
```

**What worked:** grouping identical records, ruling records out by size, and cutting Python-level work spent on every word (fewer passes, fewer imports). **What didn't:** any word order that loses frequency information, since candidates blow up.
